summary: Gives an overview of the Portable Document Format and updates the registration of application/pdf. It obsoletes RFC 3778.

plainLanguage.summary: The official label for PDF files, saying what they are.

questions: what is the application/pdf media type
subtitle: The registration of application/pdf, with an overview of PDF, its subsets and how to point into a PDF with URI fragments.

tldr.problem: The application/pdf media type was registered in RFC 3778 when PDF was an Adobe specification. PDF has since become an ISO standard, and the registration, fragment identifiers and security text were out of date.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8118 updates the registration using the RFC 6838 template, switches the change controller to ISO, summarizes PDF history and subsets, describes PDF fragment identifiers, and rewrites the security considerations.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3778 and is a largely administrative update. The fragment identifier definition now lives in ISO 32000-2, which wins if the two disagree.

today: RFC 8118 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3778. The unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it, and the RFC names ISO 32000-2 as the most recent published specification.

sections.title: What the Registration Covers
sections.content:
RFC 8118 updates the registration of the MIME media type application/pdf for documents in the Portable Document Format (PDF), and obsoletes RFC 3778.

PDF was envisioned as a way to reliably communicate and view printed information electronically across many machine configurations, operating systems and networks. It represents final-form formatted documents, with text, images, graphics and multimedia, and can carry annotations, bookmarks, file attachments, hyperlinks, metadata, encryption and digital signatures. Its imaging model was originally based on PostScript.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDF is a document that looks the same everywhere, like a photo of a page. This document updates the official label that says a file is a PDF.

sections.title: History and Subset Standards
sections.content:
The first version of PDF, 1.0, was published in 1993 by Adobe Systems Incorporated. In 2008, PDF 1.7 was adopted as the ISO standard ISO 32000-1:2008, which is technically identical to Adobe's PDF 1.7. ISO later developed a refresh, ISO 32000-2, known as PDF 2.0.

Several subset standards target specific uses: PDF/X for printing exchange, PDF/A for long-term archiving, PDF/E for engineering, PDF/VT for variable and transactional printing, and PDF/UA for accessibility. All of them use the same application/pdf media type, and one file can conform to more than one, such as PDF/A-2b and PDF/X-4. Conformance is identified through XMP metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: PDF began at one company and later became an international standard. There are special flavors for printing, archiving and accessibility, but they all share the same label.

sections.title: Fragment Identifiers
sections.content:
A fragment identifier sits at the end of a URI and points to subordinate content or sets parameters for opening it. The PDF definition first appeared in RFC 3778 and is now in ISO 32000-2; this RFC only summarizes it, and any disagreement is resolved in favor of ISO 32000-2.

A fragment has one or more name=value parameters separated by an ampersand or a pound character, processed left to right. Some identify content: page, nameddest, structelem, comment and ef (an embedded file). Others affect the view: zoom, view, viewrect, highlight and search. The fdf parameter imports data into form fields and should be the last parameter. The first page has a page value of 1, and coordinates are in 1/72 of an inch from the upper left corner of the page.
sections.plainLanguage: The part after the hash in a PDF link is like telling someone which page to open the book to and what to highlight.

sections.title: Versions and Implementations
sections.content:
PDF has been revised mostly to add features, generally in a way that older viewers fail gracefully by ignoring features they do not recognize. The older the version a file uses, the more legacy viewers support it, but the fewer features it can use. The application/pdf type is used for all versions.

The RFC says PDF viewing is built into most common platforms (iOS, OS X, Windows, Android, ChromeOS, Kindle) and browsers (Edge, Safari, Chrome, Firefox). Because the specification has been freely available since 1993, hundreds of companies and organizations make PDF tools.
sections.plainLanguage: New PDF features are added so that old readers can skip what they do not understand. Almost every device can open PDFs already.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC admits that PDF is a complex media type under RFC 6838, and that the analysis in RFC 3778 was too limited and its mitigations somewhat out of date. This update is described as primarily administrative.

PDF allows several risky constructs. Files may contain JavaScript-based scripts, refer to other PDF files, embed arbitrary files (for example through the ef action), and link to content on the Internet. The fragment directives ef and fdf can open or include additional material.

Processors should be extremely careful to prevent unwanted execution of attached executables or unpacking of attached archives, and must run scripts in a protected environment. The processor itself and its plugins can also be a source of insecurity.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDF can hide scripts and attachments, like a gift box with other things inside. Your PDF reader has to be careful and open them only in a safe space.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
The IANA section re-registers the type using the RFC 6838 template. The type is application/pdf with no required or optional parameters and binary encoding. The file extension is .pdf, the Macintosh file type code is "PDF ", and intended usage is COMMON with no restrictions.

All PDF files begin with the characters %PDF- followed by the version number, such as %PDF-1.7 or %PDF-2.0, in US-ASCII. The change controller is ISO, where it was Adobe before, reflecting the move from a proprietary specification to an open ISO standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration card says what the file type is called, how to spot it by its first characters, and who is in charge of the rules: ISO now.
